title: Operate chainsaws for limbing and logging at ground level

lessons.title: Chainsaw safety and protective clothing
lessons.html:
A chainsaw can kill

On farms chainsaws are used to clear fallen trees after storms, cut up blue gum and wattle for firewood and poles, and clean up orchards. The chain moves very fast and can cut deep into the body in a split second. Only trained and authorised people may use a chainsaw.

Kickback: the biggest danger

Kickback happens when the upper part of the bar tip (the "kickback zone") touches wood or another object. The saw is thrown up and back towards the operator's face and neck, very fast. To prevent kickback:

  • Never cut with the tip of the bar.
  • Hold the saw firmly with both hands, thumb wrapped around the front handle.
  • Keep the chain sharp and correctly tensioned.
  • Cut at high chain speed (full throttle when cutting).
  • Never cut above shoulder height.
  • Watch the tip; do not let it touch branches or the ground.

Personal protective equipment (PPE)

  • Safety helmet with face screen (visor) and ear muffs.
  • Chainsaw protective trousers or chaps. Special fibres jam the chain if it touches them.
  • Safety boots with toe caps and chainsaw protection.
  • Gloves with a good grip.
  • Close-fitting clothing; no loose scarves.

Safe work rules

  • Never work alone. Someone must be near enough to help and call for help.
  • Keep other people and animals well away from the work area.
  • Have a first aid kit with large wound dressings on site.
  • Do not use a chainsaw when tired, sick, or under alcohol or drugs.
  • Stop and rest regularly. Vibration and noise tire you.
  • Know your escape route in case a log rolls.
  • Never use the saw from a ladder or in a tree under this unit; this unit is for ground level only.

The employer must provide safe equipment and PPE under the Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993, and you must use it.

lessons.title: Parts of a chainsaw and pre-operational checks
lessons.html:
Know the parts

PartWhat it does
Engine (powerhead)Two-stroke engine that drives the chain
Guide barSteel bar the chain runs around
ChainHas cutters, depth gauges and drive links
Chain brake and front hand guardStops the chain instantly; activates by hand or by kickback
Throttle trigger and throttle lockoutThe trigger cannot be pressed unless the lockout is held
Chain catcherCatches a broken or jumped chain
Rear hand guardProtects the right hand if the chain breaks
Stop switchSwitches the engine off
Anti-vibration mountsReduce vibration to the hands
Muffler (silencer)Reduces noise and directs hot exhaust away
Chain oil pumpOils the bar and chain

Pre-operational checks

Do these checks with the engine off before every use.

  1. Chain brake works and the hand guard is not broken.
  2. Throttle lockout and trigger work and return freely.
  3. Stop switch works.
  4. Chain catcher and rear hand guard are in place.
  5. Chain is sharp, not damaged, and correctly tensioned. Pull it along the bar by hand wearing gloves: it should move freely and not hang loose under the bar.
  6. Bar is straight, the groove is clean, and nuts are tight.
  7. Muffler is in place and not damaged.
  8. Air filter is clean.
  9. Fuel and chain oil are filled.

Refuelling

  • Switch off and let the saw cool.
  • Use the fuel mix the manufacturer specifies for the two-stroke engine.
  • Refuel on bare ground, away from fire, no smoking. Wipe up spills.
  • Move away from the refuelling place before starting.

Starting safely

Put the saw on the ground on firm footing, chain brake on, chain clear of anything. Hold the front handle firmly and put your foot through the rear handle, then pull the starter. Never "drop start" the saw by pulling the cord while it hangs in the air. After starting, release the chain brake and check that the chain does not move at idle.

lessons.title: Limbing and logging at ground level
lessons.html:
Limbing

Limbing means cutting the branches off a tree lying on the ground.

  • Stand on the uphill side of the log, so it cannot roll onto you.
  • Keep the trunk between you and the saw where possible.
  • Work from the base (thick end) to the top.
  • Keep your feet firm. Clear branches from around your feet first.
  • Cut branches flush with the trunk using the bottom of the bar, never the tip.
  • Watch for branches under tension (spring poles). They can whip out when cut. Cut them in small steps from the outside, or ask your supervisor.
  • Leave branches that hold the log up until last; cutting them can make the log roll.
  • Engage the chain brake when you move more than a step or two.

Logging (cross-cutting)

Logging or cross-cutting means cutting the trunk into lengths, for example firewood or poles.

Know the tension and compression sides

  • Where a log is supported at both ends, the top is squeezed (compression) and the bottom is stretched (tension). Cut a little from the top first, then finish from the bottom, so the bar does not get pinched.
  • Where a log is supported at one end only, the top is in tension and the bottom in compression. Cut a little from the bottom first, then finish from the top.
  • If the bar gets stuck, stop the engine. Do not pull hard on the saw; use a wedge or lever to open the cut.
  • Measure lengths as instructed.
  • Do not let the chain touch the soil or stones; they blunt it fast.
  • Roll logs with a cant hook or lever, not with your hands under the log.

Basic maintenance

  • Sharpen the chain with the correct size round file and guide. File all cutters to the same length and angle. Check depth gauges.
  • Clean the bar groove and oil holes; turn the bar over regularly so it wears evenly.
  • Clean the air filter and cooling fins.
  • Check chain tension often; a new chain stretches.
  • Store the saw with a bar cover, clean and safe.

Key points

  • Never cut with the bar tip: it causes kickback.
  • Wear helmet with visor and ear muffs, chainsaw trousers, boots and gloves.
  • Check the chain brake, throttle lockout and chain before each use.
  • Start the saw on the ground with the chain brake on; never drop start.
  • Stand uphill when limbing; know tension and compression when logging.
